title: Protecting Sensitive Data
subtopics: Avoiding sensitive data in query logs
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of protecting sensitive data.
Apply data classification in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn protecting sensitive data through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Protecting Sensitive Data matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: The goal of protecting sensitive data is to reduce what identities and queries are allowed to do. Apply defense in depth: parameterize values, grant least privilege, protect sensitive data, and verify denial cases as well as allowed cases.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Data classification, Minimizing access to personal information, Data masking and redaction, Encryption responsibilities. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Data classification
items.text: Data classification helps you apply least privilege, safe parameterized access, sensitive-data protection, auditing, and database-level isolation controls. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Avoiding sensitive data in query logs
items.text: Avoiding sensitive data in query logs should be enforced at the database/application boundary rather than by UI checks alone. Bind data values as parameters, grant only the access a role needs, and test that unauthorized operations fail.

content_blocks.code: SELECT customer_id, left(email, 2) || '***' AS masked_email FROM customers ORDER BY customer_id;
content_blocks.expected_output: The expression masks email text only in this result. It is presentation-level masking, not encryption or a replacement for access control.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic data classification and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.

summary: Protecting Sensitive Data is about making the database behavior and the expected result explicit.
Use the provided subtopics as a review checklist and validate a small test case.
Keep vendor-specific syntax, access assumptions, and production-safety boundaries visible.
